<explanation>
This project is Argo Workflows – a container‐native workflow engine built as a Kubernetes CRD that orchestrates multi‐step, containerized jobs. When you’re designing a system architecture diagram for Argo Workflows, you’ll want to reflect both its distributed/microservices nature (with multiple server components and controllers) and its deep integration into the Kubernetes ecosystem.

Here are guidelines to build a comprehensive diagram that captures the system’s essential architectural elements:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Client Interfaces: Represent the various client entry points such as the Argo CLI, REST/GRPC API endpoints, and the Web UI (located under the “ui” directory). These components allow users to submit, monitor, and manage workflows.
   • Workflow Controller: The core component (in the “cmd/workflow-controller” and “server/workflow” directories) that watches Kubernetes CRDs and orchestrates workflow execution by coordinating with executors, managing retries, suspension, and termination.
   • API Server and Supporting Services: Under “server/apiserver” and “server/info”, these serve user requests and provide endpoints for configuration, logging, and access control. Also include the authentication modules (in “server/auth”) that cover service account verification, SSO, webhooks, and gatekeeper integrations.
   • Workflow Executors: The executors (in “cmd/argoexec” and related “server/artifacts”, “server/executor”) are pieces that launch container tasks in pods based on the workflow specification.
   • Artifact Management and Persistence: Represent how workflows archive results (see the “workflowarchive” and “persist/sqldb” folders) and handle artifacts (with support for multiple backends like S3, GCS, Git, etc).
   • Event Sources & Sensors: Capture the event-driven aspects (present in “server/event”, “server/eventsource” and in client libraries) that trigger workflows or integrate with external event-driven systems.
   • Custom Resources (CRDs): Depict the workflow CRDs and templates that are defined in Kubernetes and managed by the workflow controller.
   • Client Libraries: Although not explicitly services, note that the SDKs (in sdks/) for Java, Golang, and Python enable external systems to interact with Argo programmatically.

2. Map the Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Draw directional arrows from the client interfaces (CLI, UI, API clients) toward the API Server.
   • Illustrate that the API Server communicates with the Kubernetes API and then the Workflow Controller picks up new/updated workflow CRDs.
   • Show the Workflow Controller interacting with the Executor to schedule container tasks. Use arrows to denote “dispatch”, “control”, and “status reporting”.
   • Include arrows connecting the Controller to artifact handling services and the workflow archive (or persistent store) to capture output and state.
   • Indicate the authentication and authorization flow – for example, the API Server calls the authentication modules (SSO via webhooks or serviceaccounts) before processing requests.
   • Represent external integrations such as event triggers (e.g., webhooks, sensors) that feed events into the system and cause workflows to start.

3. Emphasize Design Patterns and Technologies:
   • Use a microservices or modular architecture style. Different servers (API server, workflow controller, executor, artifact server) should be shown as distinct yet interconnected modules.
   • Highlight that the system leverages Kubernetes CRDs for orchestration and uses the Kubernetes API for storing its state (backed by etcd).
   • Note key technologies: container orchestration (Kubernetes), REST/GRPC APIs, CI/CD integration, and the various client libraries.

4. Diagram Tailoring Guidelines for a Full-Stack Kubernetes Tool:
   • Clearly segregate the front-end components (UI, CLI) from back-end services (API servers, controllers, executors).
   • Use different shapes or colors to separate domain boundaries – for example, octagons for API endpoints, rounded rectangles for controller services, cylinders/stacked disks for persistence.
   • Utilize arrows with directional markers to indicate data and command flows (e.g., “Submit Workflow”, “Schedule Pod”, “Return Status”, “Archive Result”).
   • Include additional annotations that show important architectural patterns such as retry policies, DAG orchestration, and event-sourcing.
   • Create sub-diagrams if needed to drill down into specialized modules (e.g., detailed view of the authentication subsystem or executor plugin architecture).

5. Practical Drawing Steps:
   • Start with a high-level “cloud” representing the Kubernetes cluster.
   • Within the cluster, draw boxes for:
       – Client Layer: UI, CLI, API Clients.
       – API Server & Auth: A box showing the API gateway, authentication (SSO/ServiceAccount/webhook), and API endpoints.
       – Workflow Controller: The central engine that monitors CRDs and schedules tasks.
       – Executor/Artifacts: Boxes representing workflow executors that launch container pods and manage artifacts.
       – Workflow Archive & Persistence: A storage component to archive workflow data.
   • Optionally, outside of the cluster, add external services (e.g., artifact storage services like S3, Git repositories, external event sources) that integrate with Argo.
   • Annotate interactions (e.g., “Submit Workflow”, “K8s CRD Event”, “Dispatch Container”, “Return Pod Logs”) and use labels that reference file tree modules (like “server/auth”, “server/workflow”, or “ui”) as needed.

6. Final Tips:
   • Make sure every component is clearly labeled.
   • Use consistent colors and shapes to differentiate between control services, APIs, storage, and external integrations.
   • Keep the data flow directional and layered; clients at the top, middleware in the middle, and external resources at the bottom.
   • Don’t hesitate to break down complex subsystems into smaller diagrams if necessary, then reference them in an overview diagram.

Adhering to these guidelines will give you a detailed and accurate architecture diagram tailored to Argo Workflows. It will illustrate how the CLI, UI, API server, controllers, executors, artifact management, and external integrations interconnect to manage workflows on Kubernetes.

Remember, the goal is to capture all critical components and their interactions while providing clear, visual separation between the different logical layers of the system.

Happy diagramming!
</explanation>
